progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c05 (alcohol names methanol to butan-1-ol; the OH group; condensed formulas), chem-m7-c06 (fermentation of glucose by yeast from crops; ethanol from ethene and crude oil; the ethanol bottle and crude oil barrel plates), chem-m7-c03 (hydrocarbons from crude oil; octane named), chem-m5-g01 (combustion releases heat; ΔH negative; runs to completion), chem-m6-c03 (q = mcΔT, c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, "keep the digits; round at the end"; recommended prerequisite, change 10). Year 11: balancing equations; molar mass; carbon monoxide is toxic; photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide (Biology or Year 10). Not assumed: incomplete combustion as a term, energy per gram (energy density), oxidation state, carbon neutral, sociocultural (given a plain meaning).
progression.startsWith: Write alcohol combustion equations and compare fuel sources. The video opens: In Australia, E10 petrol is up to ten percent ethanol. Litre for litre, ethanol carries less energy than petrol. So why blend it in at all?
progression.stopsAfter: writing balanced complete and incomplete combustion equations for alcohols, per mole of fuel, with state symbols; explaining soot as limited oxygen; saying where data values come from and why a simple can gives a low value (reasons left to p03); explaining the steady increase in molar enthalpy of combustion with chain length; comparing fuels per gram and explaining why alcohols give less; comparing ethanol and petrol by products, carbon source, production energy, land and water; describing the economic, environmental and sociocultural implications of obtaining hydrocarbons; judging a fuel on several criteria. No molar calculation from spirit-burner data, no method, errors or risk table (chem-m7-p03).
progression.nextLesson: measuring the enthalpy of combustion of alcohols with a spirit burner (route chem-m7-p03, "Measure and compare alcohol combustion enthalpy").

teaching.task: E10 petrol is up to ten percent ethanol, yet litre for litre ethanol carries less energy than petrol. What does burning an alcohol tell us about choosing a fuel: its products, its energy per mole and per gram, and where its carbon comes from?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a fuel choice depends on energy and on where the carbon came from (1); (2) complete combustion gives CO₂ and water; balance C, H, then O, counting the alcohol's own O (2); (3) the equation is written per mole of fuel, so a half O₂ is fine; ΔH is negative because heat is released (3); (4) too little oxygen leaves carbon as CO or soot, so less energy is released; soot reports the oxygen supply (4); (5) data values come from burning a weighed fuel and measuring the heat taken in by water; a simple can catches only about half (5); (6) each CH₂ adds the same bonds to break and the same extra CO₂ and H₂O to form, so the energy per mole rises by about the same amount each time (6); (7) a bigger molecule weighs more, so fuels are compared per gram; alcohols give less per gram because the oxygen adds mass and its carbon is partly oxidised (7); (8) ethanol and petrol make the same products; the difference is whether the carbon came recently from the air or from underground (8); (9) production uses energy, land and water, so ethanol is not automatically carbon neutral (9); (10) obtaining hydrocarbons brings economic benefits with environmental and sociocultural costs, often borne by people near the site (10); (11) each fuel wins on something, so judge on several criteria (11); memory aid (12); two attempts and brief feedback (13 to 16); handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: E10 petrol is up to ten per cent ethanol, yet litre for litre ethanol carries less energy than petrol, so the video asks what burning an alcohol tells us about choosing a fuel. Complete combustion is balanced carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen, counting the oxygen the alcohol already carries; the equation is written per mole of fuel, so methanol's one and a half O2 is fine, and delta H is negative because heat is released. Too little oxygen leaves carbon as carbon monoxide or soot and releases less energy, so soot reports the oxygen supply. One recalled q = mc delta T shows where data values come from and that a simple can catches only about half. Along the series each CH2 adds the same bonds to break and the same extra products to form, so the molar enthalpy rises by about 650 kilojoules each time; per gram is the fuel comparison, and alcohols give less because the oxygen adds mass and one carbon is already partly oxidised. Ethanol and petrol give the same products, but ethanol's carbon came recently from the air; production energy, land and water mean it is not automatically carbon neutral, and obtaining hydrocarbons brings economic benefits with environmental and sociocultural costs near the site. Fuels are judged on several criteria. The memory aid is per mole, each CH2 adds about 650; per gram, oxygen costs energy. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In Australia, E10 petrol is up to ten percent ethanol. Litre for litre, ethanol carries less energy than petrol. So why blend it in at all? Burning an alcohol tells you two things that matter for choosing a fuel: how much energy you get, and where the carbon came from. So what does burning an alcohol tell us about fuel choice?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Butan-1-ol is burned in a spirit burner beneath a metal can of water. (a) Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of butan-1-ol. (b) After a few minutes, a black deposit forms on the base of the can. Explain how this deposit forms." New alcohol (the scenes balance ethanol and methanol); (b) targets the 2020 Q24 marker-reported mistake (soot blamed on the fuel without the oxygen supply, `../research/question-types-chem-m7.md`), answered positively in the feedback. Crossed mistake: "C₄H₉OH + 13/2 O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O" (the alcohol's own oxygen forgotten). (A2) "The molar enthalpy of combustion of ethanol is −1367 kJ mol⁻¹ (M = 46.07 g mol⁻¹) and of octane is −5471 kJ mol⁻¹ (M = 114.2 g mol⁻¹). (a) Calculate the energy released per gram of each fuel. (b) Compare ethanol and octane as fuels, including one advantage of ethanol that is not related to energy." Tests scene 7's unit choice and scene 8's carbon source with given data. Crossed mistake: "octane releases four times the energy per mole, so it is four times better" (the site Must Do, kJ/mol against kJ/g).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "write equations, state conditions and predict products to represent the reactions of alcohols, including but not limited to (ACSCH128, ACSCH136):; combustion; dehydration; substitution with HX; oxidation" "compare and contrast fuels from organic sources to biofuels, including ethanol" "examine the environmental, economic and sociocultural implications of obtaining and using hydrocarbons from the Earth" Only the combustion example of `C7-IQ4-04` is taught here; dehydration, substitution with HX and oxidation are chem-m7-c08a. this video starts by writing alcohol combustion equations and stops at assessing energy, production and environmental trade-offs between ethanol and petrol. It teaches: complete combustion of an alcohol to carbon dioxide and water, balanced by carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen, counting the oxygen the alcohol already carries (ethanol); the equation written per mole of fuel, with a fractional O₂ coefficient (methanol), and ΔH negative because heat is released (chem-m5-g01 recall); state symbols with liquid water for the data values; incomplete combustion when oxygen is limited, giving carbon monoxide (toxic) and soot (carbon), a yellow smoky flame and less energy released; soot as evidence about the oxygen supply; where the data values come from, through one compact recall of q = mcΔT with Codex's methanol hook dataset (0.74 g warms 100.0 g of water by 20.0 °C: 8.36 kJ, about 11 kJ per gram against about 22.7 kJ per gram in careful measurements, so the can caught about half; the reasons are chem-m7-p03); the molar enthalpies of combustion of methanol to butan-1-ol and the steady increase of about 650 kJ/mol per CH₂, explained by bonds broken and formed; energy per gram as the fuel comparison (ethanol 29.7, octane 47.9 kJ/g) and why alcohols give less (the oxygen adds mass and the carbon bonded to oxygen is already partly oxidised); about 30% less energy per litre for ethanol; same combustion products for ethanol and petrol, but recently captured carbon (fermented sugarcane, chem-m7-c06) against fossil carbon; why bioethanol is not automatically carbon neutral (production energy), and its land and water cost; the economic, environmental and sociocultural implications of obtaining hydrocarbons from the Earth; judging fuels on several criteria, with E10 as a compromise. Not here: the full molar enthalpy calculation from spirit-burner data, the set-up, the method, the error chain, improvements, validity, reliability and accuracy, and the risk table (chem-m7-p03); calculation practice and anomalous results (chem-m7-g02); bond enthalpy arithmetic (author note c; HSC Chemistry does not require it); dehydration, substitution with HX and oxidation (chem-m7-c08a); fermentation conditions (chem-m7-c06, recalled in one clause); Gibbs free energy (chem-m5-g01, recalled only for the sign); country case studies (correction 13); the bomb calorimeter (correction 11).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c05 and c06: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; oxygen brick red, the OH ringed red; O₂ molecules red pairs; CO₂ and H₂O products in a grey product box; each CH₂ in the series teal; heat as warm-orange arrows (chem-m6-c03 convention); soot specks charcoal; fossil carbon dark brown; recently captured carbon green. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Complete combustion", "Energy per gram", "Ethanol or petrol?"); centre the equation stage strip, ladder or loop, one at a time; plates small at the left or right (larger only in scenes 4, 5 and 8, where the object carries the explanation). Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous strip or plate leaves before the next draws. Reuse: `m7-ethanol-fuel-bottle-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: an amber glass bottle with a glass stopper, pale liquid, no label; hook, scene 8, handoff; coded label "ethanol"); `m7-crude-oil-barrel-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: a plain dark steel drum, no label; hook, scene 8, coded label "crude oil → petrol"); `m7-oil-gas-rig-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: an offshore platform with a derrick and crane standing in painted sea; no people visible; scene 10). Considered, not used: `m7-camping-gas-burner-v1.png` (inspected: a blue gas canister stove with a blue flame; its fuel is butane or propane, not an alcohol, so it would mislead in scenes 2 to 5); `g1-flame-v1.png` and `c7-flame-energy-v1.png` (inspected: a free-floating orange flame and a flame on a nozzle; neither shows an alcohol burning under a can); `m6-foam-cup-calorimeter-v1.png` (neutralisation, not combustion; the plate audit says so); `c8-thermometer-hot-v1.png` (a free-standing thermometer; the new set-up plate includes its own). New plates: `m7-spirit-burner-calorimeter-v1.png` and `m7-spirit-burner-calorimeter-sooty-v1.png` (shared with chem-m7-p03, which commissions the full set) and `m7-sugarcane-stalks-v1.png`; see Assets. No human figures.
